question: I got a DM saying I have pending XLM and need to sign in or pay to release it. Is that real?

golden.answer: Treat an unsolicited message that demands a payment, wallet connection or recovery credentials to release XLM as a scam signal. Do not click its link, sign anything, pay a “rectification” fee, or share a secret key or recovery phrase. Check your wallet yourself and verify any announcement through an official channel you reach independently. A legitimate claimable-balance mechanism exists, but a DM does not authenticate an offer.
keyFacts: Do not click, pay, sign, or disclose secrets because of an unsolicited message.
Not every claimable balance is a scam; a DM does not authenticate one.
Verify through your wallet or an official channel reached independently.
avoid: Do NOT tell the user to connect a wallet to the message’s site.
Do NOT say SDF asks users for private keys or deposits.
golden.notes: The independent-verification redirect is required behavior.

sources.note: Re-observed by the golden audit: "NEVER cold direct-message (DM) people to participate in airdrops and giveaways. NEVER cold DM people regarding support issues or security alerts."
Re-observed by the golden audit: "Requests to send personal and financial information ... if you think it could be real, don't click on any link ... Look up another way to contact the company"
Re-observed by the golden audit: "Claimable balances allow an account to send a payment to another account that is not necessarily prepared to receive the payment."
Re-observed by the golden audit: "Status: Final ... payment to an account that is not necessarily prepared to receive the payment."

corroboration.claim: Unsolicited demands for credentials, signatures, or payment through a message link are phishing signals; SDF says it never asks for private keys or deposits.
A legitimate claimable-balance mechanism exists independently of any unsolicited message.
